newsitem.title: USA: No punitive awards in Louisiana breast-implant case.
newsitem.headline: No punitive awards in Louisiana breast-implant case.

text.p: Louisiana women who say they received faulty breast implants made by Dow Corning Corp. will not be allowed to ask for punitive damages from Dow Chemical Co., a state district court judge has ruled.

The women, who filed a class action lawsuit against Dow Chemical (a 50 percent owner of Dow Corning), will be allowed to seek only compensatory damages, such as medical costs, from the company -- unless a higher state court overturns the ruling.

Orleans Parish District Court Judge Yada McGee ruled late Thursday without issuing oral or written reasons. Last spring, after the lawsuit was filed, the state legislature repealed the law under which the women sought punitive damages from Dow Chemical.
The old law allowed damages to be awarded as punishment in cases involving recklessly handled or transported hazardous materials.
The women claimed silicone was a hazardous substance that Dow Chemical handled recklessly. The women's attorney Walter Leger said McGee's ruling will be appealed.

The Louisiana case closely tracks similar actions brought by women in federal courts, with women claiming they suffered a variety of ailments and injuries from leaky silicone breast implants. The volume of lawsuits forced Dow Corning into bankruptcy.

The Louisiana lawsuit, which plaintiff attorneys say represented about 4,000 women, also targeted almost 100 other companies alleged to have had some role in making and distributing the implants here. McGee's ruling applies only to Dow Chemical.
A class action lawsuit filed by four Louisiana women against breast implant manufacturer Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. of New York is scheduled for trial in McGee's court Jan. 21.
